unit.title: Perform advanced welding using oxyacetylene welding process (OAW)

summary: This unit takes your oxy-acetylene welding beyond flat work on thin sheet. You will learn to plan a weld from a procedure sheet, prepare and tack joints, choose between the leftward and rightward methods, and weld sheet in the horizontal, vertical and overhead positions and small-bore pipe in fixed positions. You will also learn how cast iron, aluminium and braze welding differ from welding mild steel, how to control distortion, and how welds are inspected and tested.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It builds on the basic oxy-acetylene (OAW) unit, where you learned to set up the equipment, set a neutral flame and weld thin sheet in the flat position. Here you weld **in position** (horizontal, vertical and overhead), weld **pipe**, use the **rightward** method on thicker steel, and meet **other metals**: cast iron, aluminium and braze welding (bronze welding). You also learn to **test** welds by bending and breaking them.

Real jobs are rarely laid flat on a bench. A gate post is welded where it stands, a pipe is joined in its rack, and a bracket under a truck body is welded overhead. Oxy-acetylene is still widely used in Jamaican shops for thin-wall pipe, auto body and exhaust work, cast-iron repairs and braze welding, because it needs no power supply and gives the welder close control of the heat.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 2 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other centres who can already set up a gas welding set safely and make sound flat welds on thin sheet.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Control the extra hazards of positional and overhead welding, fluxes and fumes; keep the set leak-free and deal with backfire and flashback.
Read the welding procedure sheet or job sheet: joint, edge preparation, nozzle, filler rod, flame, method and position.
Cut, bevel and clean edges; set the root gap; line up and tack sheet and pipe so the joint holds its shape.
Choose the method to suit the thickness, and use the right torch and rod angles for each.
Make butt welds on sheet in the horizontal, vertical-up and overhead positions, controlling the pool against gravity.
Make butt welds on small-bore pipe rolled and fixed (2G, 5G, 6G), welding each half uphill in the fixed horizontal position.
Know how cast iron, aluminium and braze welding differ from mild steel: preheat, flux, filler, flame and cooling.
Use tacks, clamps, chill bars, welding sequence and the right heat to keep the job in shape.
Inspect welds by eye, carry out bend and nick-break tests, name defects and their causes, shut down safely and report faults.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety, flames, technique, positions, pipe, other metals, defects, testing and distortion.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a vertical-up (3G) butt weld on 3 mm steel sheet by the leftward method, followed by a **root bend test**; and a butt weld on small-bore steel pipe in the fixed horizontal (5G) position, welded uphill, with a cut section to show the penetration.

blocks.note: This kit does not repeat every basic step from the basic oxy-acetylene unit. If you are unsure how to assemble the set, light up or set a neutral flame, revise that unit first.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Safety and set-up for advanced work

blocks.p: The hazards of gas welding do not change when the job gets harder, but positional work, fluxes and longer jobs add to them. Hot metal falls in vertical and overhead welding, fluxes and coatings give off fumes, and a long job means more time with the set running.

head: Hazard
Why it matters on advanced jobs
How you control it
rows: Acetylene ignites very easily; a leak in a tank, pit or confined space can explode.
Every joint leak-tested with solution before lighting
Flashback arrestors and check valves fitted
Acetylene never used above about 1 bar (100 kPa, 15 psi)
Air with extra oxygen makes clothes and hair burst into flame.
Never use oxygen to freshen the air in a tank or room, or to blow dust off clothes
No oil or grease on oxygen fittings or gloves
Acetylene and copper (or alloys with a lot of copper) form a compound that can explode.
Use only fittings and pipe made for acetylene; never copper pipe
In vertical and overhead welding, sparks, drops of weld metal and hot rod ends fall onto you and the hoses.
Cap or hood, collar buttoned, leather sleeves or jacket
Stand to one side, not under the joint
Hoses kept away from where sparks fall
Hot pipe and test pieces look cold.
Glare and infrared light from the flame and pool; flux makes a very bright glare.
Gas welding goggles, about shade 4–6 (darker for a bigger flame)
Safety glasses and a face shield for grinding and cutting test strips
Fluxes, zinc from brass or bronze rods and galvanising, paint and oil all give harmful fumes.

head: Point
What to remember
rows: The acetylene is dissolved in **acetone** held in a porous filling, so the cylinder is always used and stored upright
Fuel gas fittings have **left-hand** threads (often a groove on the nut); oxygen fittings are right-hand
Just in front of the tip of the inner cone: about **3100–3200 °C** in a neutral flame
Purge the hoses, light the **acetylene first** with a spark lighter, then add oxygen until the feather just disappears
Gas welding goggles of about shade 4–6; never an arc helmet's shade 10–13, which hides the pool

blocks.p: Before an advanced job, check the set thoroughly; you will be using it for longer, and often in awkward places.

flow: Cylinders chained upright on the trolley; valves and outlets clean, with no oil, grease or damage
Regulators checked: no cracked glass or bent needles, threads sound, adjusting screws wound out
Oxygen regulator (right-hand thread) and acetylene regulator (left-hand thread) fitted firmly with the right spanner
Flashback arrestors at the regulator outlets; hoses inspected along their whole length; check valves at the torch
Nozzle chosen from the maker's chart for the metal, thickness and position; seat clean and undamaged
Stand to one side and open the cylinder valves slowly; set the working pressures from the chart
Leak-test every joint, including the cylinder valves, regulators, hose ends and torch
Purge each hose, then light the acetylene first and add oxygen to a neutral flame

blocks.p: A **backfire** is a loud pop as the flame snaps back into the nozzle and goes out or relights. It happens more in positional and pipe work, because the nozzle gets hot and close to the pool. Stop, let the nozzle cool, clean it with a **tip cleaner**, check it is tight and the pressures are right, then relight.

A **flashback** is far more dangerous: the flame burns back inside the torch and can travel up the hose into the regulator, or even the cylinder. You may hear a squeal or hiss, see smoke or sparks at the nozzle, and feel the handle getting hot.

head: Flashbacks are prevented by
If one happens
rows: Flashback arrestors at the regulators and check valves at the torch
A clean, tight nozzle that does not touch the work
Lighting up in the right order
Shut the torch valves at once, in the order the maker gives (usually oxygen first)
Let the torch cool; do not use the set until it has been checked
If a cylinder gets hot: clear the area, raise the alarm and call the fire service (110 in Jamaica)

ul: For a short stop, shut the torch off and hang it up, away from the cylinders. Never leave it lit, never lay a lit torch down, and never hang it on a regulator or cylinder.
For a longer break, close the cylinder valves as well and bleed the hoses.
If a gauge needle does not return to zero after the hoses are bled, the regulator is faulty: tag it out of use and report it.

blocks.note: Never weld or heat a drum, tank or pipe that has held fuel, oil or chemicals until a competent person has made it safe. Vapour left inside can explode, even in a container that looks empty.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Planning the weld and preparing the joint

blocks.p: On advanced work you weld to a **welding procedure sheet** (or the job sheet). It tells you exactly how the weld is to be made, so that every welder gets the same result. Read it before you start, and ask your instructor about anything that is not clear.

head: The procedure sheet gives
Example
rows: Butt joint, square edges, with the root gap stated
From the torch maker's chart for 3 mm steel; often one size smaller for vertical work
Tack spacing and the order of welding
Visual check, then a root bend test

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The deepest part of the joint, which the weld must reach and fuse
The space between the two edges at the root, before welding (also called the root opening)
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevelled edge (also called the land)
The angle cut on one edge
The total angle between the two bevelled edges of a V butt joint: two 30° bevels give a 60° included angle
A weld made in the groove between the edges of a butt joint; the G in position names such as 3G
A weld of roughly triangular section joining two surfaces at about a right angle, as in tee, lap and inside corner joints; the F in 2F
One sheet overlaps the other, and the edge of one is welded to the face of the other

blocks.h: Edge preparation for gas welding steel

head: Thickness (typical)
Preparation
Method
rows: Flanged (turned-up) edges, or square edges close together
Square edges, close together or with a small root gap
Single-V with an included angle of about 80°, with a root gap
Square edges with a gap on some plate, or a single-V of about 60°

blocks.note: These are typical figures from gas welding practice. The procedure sheet for your job always comes first: follow it and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Clean the edges and about 25 mm each side back to bright metal: rust, mill scale, paint, oil and dirt cause porosity and poor fusion.
On pipe, clean inside and out.
Set the root gap evenly along the whole joint, with a gauge, a rod of the right size or a feeler.
Check the parts are in line: no step (misalignment) between the two edges.
**Sheet:** tack each end, then at short, even spacing. Tack closer for vertical and overhead work, because heat builds up as you go and the joint moves.
**Pipe:** three or four tacks, evenly spaced round the pipe, with the line-up checked after each one.
Make tacks small and well fused, so the weld can melt them in. A cracked tack is ground out and made again, never welded over.

blocks.p: Position names use a number and a letter. **G** means a **groove** (butt) weld and **F** a fillet weld. The number gives the position.

head: Position
Plate or sheet
Pipe
rows: 1G: butt weld flat, welded from above. 1F: fillet weld flat.
1G: axis horizontal, the pipe **rolled** as you weld, so you always weld at the top
2G: plate upright, joint running horizontally. 2F: horizontal fillet.
3G: plate upright, joint running vertically. 3F: vertical fillet.
4G: butt weld overhead, welded from below. 4F: overhead fillet.
5G: axis **horizontal and fixed**; welded all round, so you pass through flat, vertical and overhead
6G: axis fixed at **45°**; welded all round

blocks.note: A pipe test passed in 6G is usually accepted as covering the other positions too, because it includes every angle of welding. That is why it is the hardest test.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: There are two ways of moving the torch and rod along a joint. A right-handed welder holds the torch in the right hand and the rod in the left.

head: Point
Leftward (forehand)
Rightward (backhand)
rows: **Forward**, at the part of the joint not yet welded
In front of the flame, dipped into the front of the pool
Behind the flame, between the flame and the finished weld
Slight side-to-side movement of the torch
Torch moves steadily along with little side movement; the rod is moved in small loops in the pool
Thin sheet, up to about 5 mm
Square edges up to a limit, then a single-V of about 60°
Neat, even finish on thin sheet
Easy control of a small pool
Smaller joint angle, so less filler rod and gas
The flame shields the hot weld as it cools, so less oxidation
Needs a wide V, so uses more rod and gas
Harder to control on thin sheet: the pool is hot and can fall through

ul: Use a **neutral flame** on mild steel. An oxidising flame burns the steel and gives a brittle, porous weld; a carburising flame adds carbon and makes it hard.
Keep the tip of the inner cone about **2–3 mm** from the pool, never touching it. The hottest part of the flame is just in front of the cone.
Keep the hot end of the rod in the outer envelope of the flame, so it stays hot and shielded, and dip it into the pool. Never melt it in the inner cone and drip it onto the work.
Watch both edges of the joint melt into the pool before you add rod. Rod added to an edge that has not melted lies on top: lack of fusion.
Keep the pool the same size all along: travel faster or ease the torch angle down if it grows; slow down if it shrinks.

blocks.p: Mild steel gas welding rods are **copper coated** to stop them rusting in store. The coating does not act as a flux, and so little of it goes into the weld that it makes no difference to the strength. Keep rods dry and clean, and use the size the procedure gives: a larger rod for thicker metal and for the rightward method.

No flux is needed for mild steel with a neutral flame, because the outer envelope of the flame keeps the air off the pool. A flux **is** needed for **cast iron**, **aluminium** and **braze welding**, where an oxide forms on the metal that the flame alone cannot remove.
Out of the flat position, gravity pulls the pool down. The rules are the same in every position: **less heat, a smaller pool, rod added where it supports the pool, and steady, comfortable working**.

head: Position
What gravity does
How you control it
rows: Horizontal butt (2G): sheet upright, joint running across
The pool sags towards the lower sheet, leaving **undercut** along the top edge and too much metal on the bottom edge
Rod added at the **top** edge of the pool
Vertical-up (3G): sheet upright, welded from the bottom upward
The pool tries to run down, sag and drip; the edges can be left with undercut
Nozzle one size smaller, or a lower torch angle
Flame pointed **up** the joint, so its pressure helps hold the pool
Rod added often at the top of the pool
Slight side-to-side movement, with a short pause at each edge
A large pool drops; sparks and hot metal fall on the welder
Keep the pool **small**: surface tension holds a small pool up, a big one drips
Flame pointed slightly in the direction of travel
Rod added often to support the pool
Stand to one side; full PPE

blocks.h: Vertical-up butt weld on 3 mm sheet (the 3G test)

flow: Clean the edges, set the root gap from the procedure and tack the sheets, with tacks closer than for flat work
Fix the test piece upright in a positioner or clamp, at a height where you can reach the whole joint comfortably
Set a neutral flame with the nozzle the procedure gives for vertical work
Start at the bottom: hold the flame until both edges melt into a small pool
Point the flame upward along the joint and add rod at the top edge of the pool
Move upward steadily with a slight side-to-side movement, pausing briefly at each edge so both edges fuse with no undercut
If the pool grows or sags, lower the torch angle or move up a little faster
Finish at the top by filling the crater, then lift the flame away slowly

blocks.note: Heat builds up as you climb, so the top of the joint gets hotter than the bottom. Watch the pool and ease the torch angle down as you go. Rest your arm against something steady.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Wear a cap or hood, button your collar, and wear leather sleeves or a jacket, gauntlets and boots with trousers over them.
Clear anything that can burn from beneath the work, including the hoses.
Set the job at a height where you can reach the whole joint without stretching, and **stand to one side of the joint, not directly under it**.
Tack closely and clamp securely: an overhead joint that moves is very hard to recover.
Keep the pool small, add rod often, and travel steadily so both edges fuse without the pool sagging.
Rest your arm when you need to, and stop before you tire: a shaking hand spoils the weld and drops the pool.
Tack closely; the lower sheet takes more of the weld metal, so keep the pool small.
Aim the flame slightly upward and add the rod at the top edge of the pool, so metal goes where gravity takes it away.
Watch the top edge for undercut and the bottom edge for sagging metal that has not fused (overlap).

blocks.note: In every position, a pool that grows too big will fall. When it starts to sag, take the heat away for a moment by moving on or lifting the flame slightly; do not chase it with more rod.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Oxy-acetylene is well suited to small-bore steel pipe with thin walls, such as the 50–60 mm pipe with a 3 mm wall used in the practical test. The pipe is either **rolled** (1G), so you always weld at the top, or **fixed** (2G, 5G, 6G), so you move round it.

flow: Cut both pipe ends **square** and check them with a square or a **wraparound** (a strip of card or thin sheet wrapped round the pipe as a guide)
Prepare the ends as the procedure says: thin-wall pipe can be square-edged; thicker wall is bevelled
Clean the ends inside and out to bright metal for about 25 mm
Lay the two lengths in a piece of **angle iron**, or in a jig, so they line up straight, with an even root gap all round
Tack in three or four places, evenly spaced, checking the line-up and the gap after each tack
Fix the pipe in a stand at a comfortable height (often about chest height); in a fixed position it must **not** be turned while you weld

blocks.h: Welding a fixed horizontal pipe (5G) uphill

blocks.p: Think of the joint as a clock face. The bottom is 6 o'clock, the top 12 o'clock and the sides 3 and 9 o'clock. In the 5G position you weld round the pipe in two halves, each one **uphill**, from the bottom to the top.

head: Part of the pipe
You are welding
Watch for
rows: Pool dropping; keep it small; stand to the side
Too much heat building up; burn-through

flow: Start the first half just past the bottom (a little beyond 6 o'clock), melt in, and weld up one side
Keep changing your body position and the torch angle as you go round, so the flame and rod stay at the right angles to the pipe surface
Fuse fully into each tack as you reach it
Finish the first half just past the top (a little beyond 12 o'clock)
Start the second half by melting back into the start of the first half at the bottom, then weld up the other side
Finish by melting into the end of the first half at the top, so the starts and finishes overlap; fill the crater
Let the pipe cool in air, then clean and inspect it all round

blocks.note: Never stand directly under the pipe when you weld the bottom. Keep the hoses away from the hot pipe and from where sparks fall, and wear full PPE, with your collar buttoned and a cap on for the overhead part.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **1G rolled:** weld a short length at the top, stop, roll the pipe, and carry on, so the weld is always flat. The quickest and easiest pipe weld.
**2G:** the pipe stands upright and the joint runs round it horizontally. It is welded like a horizontal butt weld on sheet: small pool, rod at the top edge.
**6G:** the pipe is fixed at 45°. It combines all the angles and is the hardest position.

blocks.note: Even penetration all round is the aim. In the practical, the instructor cuts a section through one joint so the group can see how far the weld has fused through the wall.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Cast iron, aluminium and braze welding

blocks.p: Mild steel is the easiest metal to gas weld: it glows red before it melts, and a neutral flame needs no flux. Other metals behave differently.

head: Point
Fusion welding mild steel
Fusion welding cast iron
Fusion welding aluminium
Braze welding (bronze welding) steel or cast iron
rows: **No**: it is heated to a dull red, well below its melting point
Aluminium rod to suit the alloy
Neutral, or very slightly carburising, as the procedure says
The whole casting, slowly, and kept hot while welding
Thick parts warmed, to stop the heat being drawn away
The joint area to the right heat for the bronze to wet it
Cool **very slowly**: in a furnace, under an insulating blanket, or buried in dry sand or lime
Wash all flux off with **hot water and a brush**
Let it cool; clean off the flux

blocks.p: Grey cast iron is **brittle**. It cannot stretch, so uneven heating and cooling crack it. That is why the whole casting is preheated slowly, kept hot while it is welded, and then cooled very slowly. A casting heated in one spot, or cooled quickly in a breeze or with water, will crack beside the weld. Many cast-iron repairs are braze welded instead, because the casting is not melted and needs much less heat.

ul: Aluminium melts at only about 660 °C, far lower than steel, and it **shows no colour change** before it melts. It looks the same until it suddenly collapses.
Its surface is covered with a tough **oxide skin** that melts at over 2000 °C. A flux is needed to break up this skin so the metal can fuse.
Aluminium conducts heat away very fast, so thick parts need warming first, then the pool forms quickly once it starts.
Support the joint well: hot aluminium is weak and sags.
Aluminium fluxes are **corrosive**. Wash every trace off straight after welding with hot water and a stiff brush, or the joint will corrode.
The flux fumes irritate the nose and lungs: work with good ventilation.

blocks.p: In braze welding, the parent metal is **heated but not melted**. A brass or bronze rod, which melts at a much lower temperature than steel or cast iron, is melted onto the hot, fluxed surface. The molten bronze **wets** (tins) the clean surface, spreading into a thin film and bonding to it, and the joint is then built up like a weld. It is used for repairing cast iron, joining thin steel with less heat and distortion, and joining different metals.

flow: Prepare the joint (a V on thicker parts) and clean it to bright metal: bronze will not wet a dirty, rusty or greasy surface
Set a slightly oxidising flame and heat the joint to a dull red
Dip the hot rod in flux and melt a little onto the joint; watch it flow and wet (tin) the surface
Build up the joint, keeping the surface tinned ahead of the pool
Let it cool, then clean off the flux residue

blocks.note: Brass and bronze rods contain **zinc**. If the joint gets too hot, the zinc boils off as white fumes (zinc oxide) and leaves holes. The fumes can give you metal fume fever. Keep the heat down and work with good ventilation. A slightly oxidising flame helps by forming a skin that holds the zinc in.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: A braze-welded joint loses strength if it gets hot in service (above about 250 °C), so it is not used on parts that run hot.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Preheating** warms the part before welding, so the weld and the metal around it cool more slowly and evenly. **Stress relieving** is a heat treatment after welding: the whole part is heated evenly to a set temperature (for carbon steel often about 600–650 °C), held there, then cooled slowly. It removes the stresses locked into the part as the weld shrank. The procedure sheet gives the temperatures.

When metal is heated it expands, and as the weld cools it **shrinks**, pulling the parts with it. Thin sheet buckles, butt joints close up or bow, and tee joints pull out of square. This is **distortion**.
Gas welding usually causes **more distortion** in sheet than arc welding. Oxy-acetylene is slower, so heat has time to spread over a wide area of the sheet, and more metal expands and then shrinks.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Holds the edges in line and the gap even while the weld is made
Holds the parts firmly in shape while they cool
Copper or aluminium bars clamped beside the joint draw heat away, so less of the sheet gets hot
Short runs are made in the opposite direction to the overall progress, each ending where the last began, so the heat is spread out
Short runs are made at spaced points along the joint, then the gaps are filled in
Opposite sides or ends are welded in turn so the pulls cancel
The parts are set slightly out of line, so the shrinking weld pulls them straight
On a long seam in sheet, the gap is set a little wider at the far end, because the edges close up as the weld moves along
The right nozzle from the chart and a steady speed: extra heat and extra weld metal mean extra shrinking

blocks.note: Throwing water on a weld does not stop it shrinking, and on some steels and on cast iron it causes cracking. Let welds cool in air unless the procedure says otherwise.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: If a part has distorted, do not hammer it cold. Tell your instructor, who will decide whether it can be corrected or must be made again.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Inspection, testing and finishing the job

blocks.p: The **first check on every weld is a visual check**. Clean the weld with a wire brush and look at it in good light, with a magnifying glass if needed. Measure sizes with a rule or weld gauge.

ul: **Face:** even width and height, even **ripples** (the ridges left as the pool freezes), smooth blending into the plate at both edges.
**No** undercut, overlap, cracks, porosity, burnt surface or unfilled crater.
**Back of a butt weld:** an even penetration bead along the full length, with no burn-through and no unmelted edges.
**The job:** still flat, square and in line; pipe still straight.

head: Defect
What it is
Common causes
Prevention
rows: Weld metal lying on the edge or on the previous run without melting into it
Too little heat; nozzle too small
The weld has not reached through the root
Correct gap and nozzle; steady speed
A hole melted right through the joint
Too much heat; nozzle too big
Too much metal hanging through the root
A groove melted at the edge of the weld and left unfilled
No pause or rod at the edges
Pause and add rod at the edges
Weld metal spilled over the plate without fusing to it
Smaller pool; rod at the top edge
Lines in or beside the weld
Fast or uneven cooling (especially cast iron)
Preheat and cool slowly where needed
A hollow at the end of a run
Add rod and lift the flame away slowly
One edge higher than the other
Line up and tack carefully; check before welding

blocks.p: Test pieces are cut and bent or broken to see inside the weld. Strips are cut **across** the weld, usually about 25 mm wide, by the method the Centre allows.

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: The strip is bent round a former or in a vice with the **face** of the weld on the outside of the bend
Faults near the face: lack of fusion at the edges, porosity, cracks
The strip is bent with the **root** on the outside
Whether the root has fused right through. A good weld bends without cracking or opening up.
A small notch (nick) is cut in the weld and the strip is broken across it
The broken face shows the inside of the weld: gas holes, unmelted edges (shiny, smooth areas), inclusions
A section is cut across the weld and the face is smoothed (and sometimes etched)
The shape of the weld and how far it has penetrated

blocks.note: Wear safety glasses and a face shield when cutting, grinding and bending test strips, and stand to the side of the vice. Test strips can spring out or snap. Record every result on the test sheet.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Shut the torch off in the maker's order, close the cylinder valves, bleed the hoses to zero and wind out the adjusting screws.
Coil the hoses, clean and store the nozzles with the right-sized tip cleaner, and leave the cylinders chained upright.
Put hot test pieces where no one will pick them up, marked HOT, and check the area for smouldering.
Report faulty equipment (leaks, damaged hoses, a gauge that does not return to zero, repeated backfires, any flashback), injuries and near misses, and record your work on the job card or test sheet.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a welding procedure sheet and say what each item means for the job.
I can control the extra hazards of positional, overhead and flux work, and explain why oxygen must never be used to freshen the air.
I can check, assemble and leak-test the set, and say what to do in a backfire or flashback.
I can name the parts of a joint: root, root gap, root face, bevel angle and included angle.
I can choose the edge preparation and method to suit the thickness.
I can compare leftward and rightward welding: direction, angles, thickness, advantages.
I can name the welding positions 1G to 6G and 1F to 4F.
I can weld sheet in the horizontal, vertical-up and overhead positions, controlling the pool.
I can prepare, line up and tack small-bore pipe, and weld it in the 5G position uphill.
I can explain how cast iron, aluminium and braze welding differ from welding mild steel.
I can explain why gas welding distorts sheet, and use tacks, clamps, chill bars and welding sequence to control it.
I can inspect a weld by eye and name the common defects, with their causes and prevention.
I can describe face bend, root bend and nick-break tests and what they show.
I can shut down safely and report faults.

terms: Back-step welding
Welding short runs back towards the start, each ending where the last began, to spread the heat
Backfire
A loud pop as the flame snaps back into the nozzle
Braze welding
Joining with a brass or bronze rod without melting the parent metal; also called bronze welding
Chill bar
A copper or aluminium bar clamped beside a weld to draw heat away
Crater
The hollow left at the end of a run if it is not filled
Distortion
Bending or pulling out of shape as a weld cools and shrinks
Face bend
A bend test with the weld face on the outside of the bend
Fillet weld
A roughly triangular weld joining two surfaces at about a right angle
Flashback
The flame burning back inside the torch and into the hose
Flux
A powder or paste that removes oxides and protects the metal; needed for cast iron, aluminium and braze welding
Groove weld
A weld in the groove between the edges of a butt joint; the G in 3G
Included angle
The total angle between the two bevelled edges of a V butt joint
Lap joint
One sheet overlapping another, the edge of one welded to the face of the other
Leftward welding
Welding right to left with the flame pointing forward and the rod in front; for thin sheet
Nick-break test
A test in which a notched weld strip is broken to show the inside of the weld; a fracture test
Preheat
Warming the part before welding so it cools slowly and evenly
Rightward welding
Welding left to right with the flame pointing back at the weld and the rod behind it; for steel over about 5 mm
Ripples
The even ridges on the face of a weld, left as the pool freezes
Root
The deepest part of the joint
Root bend
A bend test with the weld root on the outside of the bend
Root face
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevelled edge
Root gap
The space between the edges at the root before welding
Stress relieving
Heating a welded part evenly and cooling it slowly to remove locked-in stresses
Tinning
The molten bronze wetting and spreading in a thin film on the hot, clean surface
Tip cleaner
A small wire file used to clean the gas holes of a nozzle
Uphill welding
Welding upward, from the bottom of the joint to the top
Wraparound
A strip wrapped round a pipe to mark or check a square end
1G to 6G
Position names for groove (butt) welds; for pipe, 5G is fixed horizontal and 6G fixed at 45°

c1.title: Vertical-up practice in Port Antonio
c1.text: At a training centre in Port Antonio, Portland, Dwight is practising vertical-up (3G) butt welds on 3 mm mild steel sheet by the leftward method. He has fitted the same nozzle he used for his flat welds. He tacked the 150 mm joint only at its two ends. As he moves up, the gap narrows, the pool sags and drips, and grooves are left along both edges of the weld.

c2.title: An overhead patch in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Melissa works at a garage in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. She is gas welding a sheet-steel patch onto the underside of a steel tool box bolted to a truck, so the joint is overhead. The truck's diesel tank is about a metre from the box. Because of the heat she has opened her collar and rolled up her sleeves. She stands directly under the joint, and the oxygen and acetylene hoses lie on the ground beneath the work.

c3.title: Pipe for a pump stand in Christiana
c3.text: On a farm near Christiana, Manchester, Shamar is building a stand for an irrigation pump from 50 mm steel pipe with a 3 mm wall. He must join two lengths with a butt weld in the fixed horizontal (5G) position, because the pipe will already be held in the stand. He cut the ends with a hacksaw by eye, and they are not square. He plans to hold the two lengths together by hand while he tacks them.

c4.title: A cracked cast-iron bracket in Linstead
c4.text: A mechanic in Linstead, St Catherine, brings a cracked grey cast-iron bracket from a sugar-cane juice machine to a small fabrication shop. The shop decides to braze weld it rather than fusion weld it. The trainee, Kemoy, grinds a V along the crack. While he is working, white smoke rises from the molten bronze, and the bronze will not spread over one dark, greasy patch.

c5.title: Test day in Morant Bay
c5.text: At a training centre in Morant Bay, St Thomas, Andrea's group is checking the week's oxy-acetylene welds. A long butt seam in 1.2 mm sheet has buckled, and its gap closed up near the far end as it was welded. A nick-break specimen from a 3 mm butt weld shows smooth, shiny, unmelted edge surfaces inside the weld. Another strip is to be bent to check the face side of a weld.

questions.q: Which change to the heat would help Dwight most?
o: Fit a larger nozzle so that the pool sets more quickly
Turn the oxygen up so the flame burns hotter and faster
Fit a nozzle one size smaller, or lower the torch angle
Hold the inner cone closer, touching the top of the pool
questions.why: In the vertical position the pool sags if it gets too big and hot. A nozzle one size smaller than for flat work, or a lower torch angle, puts less heat into the pool so it stays small.

questions.q: Where should Dwight add the filler rod to help hold the pool up?
o: At the bottom of the pool, below the flame
At the top edge of the pool, adding it often
Ahead of the pool, on the cold sheet above it
Only at the end of the joint, to fill the crater
questions.why: Rod added often at the top of the pool cools it a little and gives it something to sit on. Rod laid on cold sheet ahead of the pool does not fuse.

questions.q: Why should the joint have had more tacks, closer together?
o: Extra tacks add filler metal, so less rod is needed later
Close tacks keep the sheet cool, so the pool cannot sag
More tacks mean the edges need not be cleaned first
Heat builds as he climbs, so the joint moves and closes
questions.why: As the weld moves up, the sheet heats and expands, and the gap ahead of the pool closes or opens. Close tacks hold the gap and the line of the joint.

questions.q: What should Dwight do about the grooves along both edges of the weld?
o: Pause briefly at each edge and add rod there
Weave wider and faster, without stopping at the edges
Point the flame downward to push the pool to the edges
Grind the grooves out after welding and leave them open
questions.why: The grooves are undercut: the edges melted but were not filled. A short pause at each edge, with rod added there, fills the edge before the pool moves on.

questions.q: Where should Melissa stand while she welds?
o: Directly under it, so she can see the pool clearly
On the truck's bumper, close above the joint
To one side of the joint, not directly under it
Behind the cylinders, as far back as the hoses reach
questions.why: Sparks, drops of weld metal and hot rod ends fall straight down in overhead welding. Standing to one side keeps them off her while she can still reach and see the joint.

questions.q: Why should the hoses be moved from the ground beneath the work?
o: Falling hot metal and sparks can burn through them
The gas flows more slowly when the hoses lie flat
The hoses cool the joint above them and cause cracks
Hoses lying flat make the regulators read too high
questions.why: Hot metal falling from an overhead weld can burn through a hose and release gas next to the flame. Run the hoses away from where sparks fall.

questions.q: What must be done about the truck's diesel tank before she lights up?
o: Nothing, as diesel does not catch fire the way petrol does
Shield it from sparks and heat, with an extinguisher ready
Fill it right up so that there is less vapour in the tank
Run the engine so the fuel moves and cannot get hot
questions.why: Fuel, fuel lines and anything that burns near the work must be shielded from sparks and heat, or the part removed and welded on the bench, with an extinguisher at hand and a fire watch afterwards.

questions.q: What should Shamar do first about the pipe ends?
o: Leave them, as the weld will fill any gaps that are left
Heat them red and hammer them flat against each other
Bevel them steeply so the uneven gap no longer matters
File them square, checking with a square or wraparound
questions.why: Ends that are not square give an uneven gap: too wide in one place for the pool, too tight in another for penetration. Square them and check with a square or a wraparound before cleaning.

questions.q: How should the two lengths be lined up for tacking?
o: Held together by hand, ends touching, while he tacks
Laid straight in angle iron, with an even gap all round
Stood on end on the floor, one length on top of the other
Clamped in the stand straight away, then lined up by eye
questions.why: Angle iron (or a jig) holds both lengths straight and in line while the gap is set and the tacks are made. Holding them by hand lets them move, and puts the hand next to the flame.

questions.q: As Shamar welds from the bottom of the pipe up one side, what must he keep doing?
o: Change his body and torch position to keep the angles right
Turn the pipe a little at a time so he always welds on top
Hold the torch at the same fixed angle to the floor
Speed up near the bottom, where the pool is easiest to hold
questions.why: The pipe surface curves away from him, so a fixed torch angle soon becomes wrong. He keeps moving his body, wrist and torch so the flame and rod stay at the same angles to the joint.

questions.q: How should the second half of the weld meet the first half?
o: It stops a few millimetres short, so the halves do not touch
It is laid over the top of the first half for its full length
It melts into the first half's start and end, overlapping them
It runs from the top down, to meet the first half at the bottom
questions.why: The second half starts by melting back into the start of the first half at the bottom and finishes by melting into its end at the top. Overlapping the starts and finishes leaves no unfused gap.

questions.q: Why did the shop choose braze welding for this cast-iron repair?
o: Less heat goes in, so the casting is less likely to crack
Bronze matches the colour of cast iron once it is painted
Braze welding needs no cleaning, flux or heat on the part
Cast iron cannot be joined by any welding process at all
questions.why: Cast iron is brittle and cracks with uneven heating and cooling. In braze welding the casting is only heated to a dull red, not melted, so far less heat goes in.

questions.q: What does the white smoke rising from the bronze tell Kemoy?
o: The flux has finished its work and he can stop adding it
The bronze is overheating and its zinc is boiling off
The flame is too small and he should fit a bigger nozzle
The casting is now cool enough to start adding bronze
questions.why: White smoke from brass or bronze is zinc oxide: the joint is too hot and zinc is boiling out, which leaves holes and gives harmful fumes. He should reduce the heat and keep good ventilation.

questions.q: Why will the bronze not spread over the greasy patch?
o: Grease holds heat in, so the patch is far too cold for bronze
Greasy cast iron melts long before the bronze rod does
Bronze needs a thin film of grease to flow, but not that much
Bronze only wets clean metal, and grease stops it bonding
questions.why: Braze welding depends on the bronze wetting (tinning) a clean, fluxed surface. Grease, rust and dirt stop it bonding, so the joint must be cleaned to bright metal first.

questions.q: What could Andrea do on the next long sheet seam so the gap does not close up?
o: Leave out the tacks so that the edges can move freely
Set the gap a little wider at the far end before tacking
Weld the seam in one long run with a larger, hotter nozzle
Cool each finished part of the seam at once with a wet rag
questions.why: On a long seam the edges close up ahead of the weld as the sheet heats. Setting the gap slightly wider at the far end (a tapered gap), with close tacks, allows for this.

questions.q: What fault do the shiny, unmelted edge surfaces in the nick-break show?
o: Porosity, from an oxidising flame and a dirty joint
Undercut at the toes, from too steep a torch angle
Excess penetration, from too wide a root gap
Lack of fusion: the edges were never melted in
questions.why: A smooth, shiny area on a broken weld is the original edge of the plate: weld metal lay against it without melting it. Gas holes would show as round cavities instead.

questions.q: How is a strip bent to check the face side of the weld for faults?
o: With the face of the weld on the outside of the bend
With the root of the weld on the outside of the bend
Heated red first, so that it bends without any force
Twisted in the vice, so that both sides are stretched
questions.why: A bend stretches the outside surface, so faults on that side open up. For a face bend, the face is on the outside; for a root bend, the root is.

questions.q: Why will aluminium not fuse properly under the flame unless a flux is used?
o: It melts far hotter than steel, so the flame cannot reach it
Its oxide skin melts far hotter than the metal under it
It glows red too early, and the edges burn away
Its filler rod rusts in store unless flux protects it
questions.why: Aluminium melts at about 660 °C, but its oxide skin melts at over 2000 °C and would stop the metal fusing. The flux breaks up the oxide; it must be washed off afterwards because it is corrosive.

questions.q: A pipe is fixed with its axis vertical, and the joint is welded all round in a horizontal line. Which position is this?
o: 1G
5G
6G
2G
questions.why: 2G pipe stands upright with the weld running round it horizontally. 1G is rolled, 5G is fixed with the axis horizontal, and 6G is fixed at 45°.

questions.q: Owen is rightward welding 6 mm steel plate. Where should his filler rod be?
o: In front of the flame, ahead of the weld pool
Under the plate, held against the back of the joint
Behind the flame, between it and the finished weld
Inside the inner cone, melting off in drops
questions.why: In rightward welding the flame points back at the weld and the rod follows behind the flame. The flame also shields the hot weld as it cools.
